newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Sharansky back to land that branded him a traitor.
newsitem.headline: Sharansky back to land that branded him a traitor.

text.p: Natan Sharansky last saw Moscow through the windows of a KGB car on his way to jail for wanting to go to Israel.
Next week he will return to the Russian capital in a limousine as a minister of the Jewish state.
Sharansky will head a trade mission to the former Communist country that branded him a traitor for fighting for Soviet Jewish emigration.
Sharansky's Gulag ordeal ended when he crossed the Glienicke Bridge from East to West Berlin in 1986 and flew to Israel as a hero.

He turned down an invitation for a return visit after the collapse of the Soviet Union. But his new political career as Trade and Industry Minister in Benjamin Netanyahu's government has changed his mind.
"The fact is, of course, I didn't have any nostalgic feelings and I didn't feel any real reason to go," he said.

"Now somehow, when you have become a minister and you are interested as a minister to open new markets...you have a practical reason to go. Then also, you feel some kind of curiosity about it," he told Reuters in an interview.

Sharansky, 49, was one of the most celebrated Soviet dissidents in the West. Fluent in English and a wit, he made a stand-out spokesman. His wife Avital campaigned on diplomatic doorsteps the world over until his release on February 11, 1986, in an East-West prisoner swap.
Last May, buoyed by immigrants from the former Soviet Union, Sharansky's Yisrael ba-Aliya (Israel of Immigration) party came out of nowhere to win seven seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset.
After a decade of shunning Israeli politics, he now finds himself returning to Moscow on Sunday at the head of a team of 60 businessmen on a five-day visit to boost commercial ties.
Despite the mission's formal business side, it is also charged with emotion. Sharansky last saw Moscow the day of his arrest by KGB agents two decades ago.

"I remember 20 years ago, the day when I was arrested -- the 13th of March 1977. They put me in the car, they took me and I understood the KGB was taking me to the prison. And it was just published in the newspaper that I was accused of being an American spy.

"So I remember that I was saying to myself in the car, 'Look in the streets, you are seeing Moscow for the last time'. And I tried to look and then I didn't remember anything. Where I was, really it was like a shock. So ever since then, I didn't see Moscow and I am sure it will be very different," he said.
Politically the climate changed as far back as 1991 when Moscow "rehabilitated" him, and last year it officially hailed the start of his government career.
But some things never change in the land where he was known as Anatoly Shcharansky. "Nyet" was the response to his request to visit the labour camp where he was imprisoned.
"They are embarrassed," he said. "I asked for the labour camp. They said no. They are looking for a pretext not to let me, and I think somehow they'd like to avoid this part."
"You know it has changed but not to the end," he said.
Sharansky could get back the Russian citizenship revoked on the day of his release. But he said he didn't need it.
He insisted he harbours no hostility and seeks no revenge.

"If I left defeated or humiliated, probably I would feel very revengeful but the thing is that I always felt -- and definitely after the visit -- that really it was a great victory and they lost. They were destroyed," he said.

His talks with Russian officials will focus on agricultural technology, medical equipment and telecommunications. Israeli officials say bilateral trade, virtually non-existent five years ago, is now worth about $500 million and expanding fast.
Sharansky's mother Ida Milgrom, who left the Soviet Union six months after he did, will go to Moscow with him.

Regarded by Israelis as a centrist, Sharansky is willing to swap land for peace but in return for Arab commitments to human rights and democracy. He backed Netanyahu's self-rule deal on the West Bank town of Hebron last week but demanded a reciprocal Palestinian commitment to pursue peace.

Asked if Moscow, co-sponsor with the United States of Middle East peace moves, could play a role in resolving Israel's conflict with the Arabs, he said: "It can. If it will want to do it so much that it will change its attitude, relations with Iran and so on, it might be. But not immediately. It still has a big way to go."
